title: Weather and seasons
goal: Talk about the weather in sentences with no subject, name the four seasons with their endings, and tell "it's cold" apart from "I'm cold".
bekal: answer *Milyen az idő?* with ten ready-made sentences
give temperatures in degrees, including below zero
use *tavasszal, nyáron, ősszel, télen* to say "in" a season

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Az első tél
dialogs.intro: Early January, outside the language school. Budi's first snow fell last night.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Igen, nagyon hideg. Hány fok van?
lines.id: Yes, very cold. How many degrees is it?
lines.literal: yes, very cold. how-many degree is?

lines.speaker: Anna:
lines.id: Minus five. And it's snowing too.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Indonéziában soha nincs hó. Ez az első telem.
lines.id: It never snows in Indonesia. This is my first winter.
lines.literal: Indonesia-in never not-is snow. this the first winter-my.

lines.speaker: Anna:
lines.id: Really? And do you like winter?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Szeretem, de fázom. Nálunk mindig meleg van.
lines.id: I do, but I'm cold. It's always hot back home.
lines.literal: I-like-it, but I-am-cold. at-us always hot is.

lines.speaker: Anna:
lines.id: How warm is it in Jakarta?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Harminc fok, egész évben. Két évszak van: száraz és esős.
lines.id: Thirty degrees, all year round. There are two seasons: dry and rainy.
lines.literal: thirty degree, whole year-in. two season is: dry and rainy.

lines.speaker: Anna:
lines.text: Nálunk négy évszak van. A tavasz a legszebb.
lines.id: We have four seasons. Spring is the most beautiful.
lines.literal: at-us four season is. the spring the most-beautiful.

lines.speaker: Anna:
lines.text: Márciusban. Akkor süt a nap, és minden virágzik.
lines.id: In March. Then the sun shines and everything blooms.
lines.literal: March-in. then it-shines the sun, and all it-blooms.

notes: **Hideg van — a sentence with no subject.** Literally "cold is", without saying who or what is cold. Hungarian uses this pattern for all weather talk, where English needs a dummy "it": "it's cold".

**Hideg van is not Fázom.** Keep this distinction tidy: *Hideg van* means **the weather** is cold, while *Fázom* means **I** feel cold. Both can be true at once, as in the dialogue. The opposite pair: *Meleg van* (it's hot) versus *Melegem van* (I'm hot).

**Havazik and esik az eső.** "It's snowing" is a single verb, *havazik*. "It's raining" takes two words: *esik az eső* — literally "the rain falls". The short form *esik* alone is also used and heard very often.

**Ez az első telem** shows *tél* shortening its vowel once an ending is added: *tél* → *telem*, *telet*, *télen*. You've already seen the same thing with *víz* → *vizet* in unit 7 and *nyár* → *nyarat*.

**Nálunk means "at our place, where we live"** — the *-nál* ending from unit 12 plus a possessive ending. Hungarians use it for their country, their town, or their home, depending on context. Its siblings are *nálatok* (at your place, plural) and *náluk* (at their place).
**A legszebb** uses the prefix *leg-* to say "most". It goes together with the ending *-bb*: *szép* → *szebb* (more beautiful) → *legszebb* (most beautiful). The full rule is in unit 16.

grammars.title: Weather: ten sentences that cover it all
body: Almost all of them use *van* with no subject, or a single verb.
after: **Temperatures use fok.** *Húsz fok van* (twenty degrees), *mínusz öt fok van* (minus five degrees), *Hány fok van?* (how many degrees is it?). Note that *fok* stays singular after a number, like every other noun.
*Idő* means both "time" and "weather". Beginners may therefore misread *Milyen az idő?* as "what time is it" — but Hungarian uses *Hány óra van?* for that, so the confusion never lasts long.

grammars.title: Is it cold, or are you cold?
body: Hungarian keeps apart two things that are easy to blur.
after: *Fázik* is an *-ik* verb: *fázom, fázol, fázik, fázunk, fáztok, fáznak*. *Melegem van*, on the other hand, is built from a possessive ending: literally "my-heat is" — the same pattern as *Nincs pénzem* from unit 5.

The first pattern is used for many bodily states: *Éhes vagyok* (hungry), *Szomjas vagyok* (thirsty), *Álmos vagyok* (sleepy), *Fáradt vagyok* (tired), but *Melegem van* and *Hidegem van* take the other road. Learn the two as a pair.

grammars.title: The four seasons and their endings
body: Note that "in a season" doesn't use a place ending but the "with" ending — an old habit you simply memorize.
after: *Tavasszal* and *ősszel* use the *-val/-vel* ending with its merged *v*, while *nyáron* and *télen* use the surface ending *-on/-en*. There's no logic to explain; these four forms are learned whole, and luckily there are only four.

In Hungary the seasons are truly different from one another: summer can reach 35 degrees, winter drops to minus 10. For newcomers from the tropics, *ősz* — autumn — is usually the most pleasant, and *november* the hardest, foggy and dark from four in the afternoon.

blocks.text: One sentence that will come in very handy in November: *Hozz esernyőt!* — "Bring an umbrella!". And one for January: *Vegyél fel kabátot!* — "Put on a coat!". Both are imperatives, which you'll learn at A2; for now, just recognize them.

head: Months
Typical weather
What's going on
rows: *karácsony* (Christmas), the Christmas market on Vörösmarty tér
*tavasz*, the city turns green, cafés open their terraces
*nyár*, people head to Lake Balaton and the pools
*ősz*, the best leaf colors, then November fog

blocks.text: *Szia, hogy vagy? Milyen idő van nálatok?* — the safest small-talk question in all of Hungary, and now you can answer it fully. Weather opens conversations here just as in Britain; the difference is that Hungarians will follow up straight away with a very detailed complaint.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the right form of the season.
Choose: weather or person. Write the Hungarian sentence.
Spaced review — unit 11. Translate into Hungarian without looking back at the unit.
